Ganesan Internet-Draft 15 November 2026 Intended status: Standards Track Expires: 19 May 2027 Agent Authenticator: Hardware-Bound, Origin-Bound Authentication for AI Agents draft-ganesan-agent-authenticator-00 Abstract This document specifies the Agent Authenticator, a mechanism that lets autonomous software agents, such as AI coding agents, authenticate to services with properties comparable to passkeys: keys held in secure hardware, no shared secrets, binding to the service's origin that a manipulated agent cannot override, attested execution environments, and explicit human approval of each agent and of high- risk actions. The same protocol serves agents on personal computers and in cloud environments. It is a profile over existing mechanisms rather than a new identity system: it uses OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, the Identity Assertion JSON Web Token (JWT) Authorization Grant, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) authorization, and it binds each agent action to a signed, tamper-evident record. Introduction Software agents built on large language models increasingly act on behalf of people when using services such as code hosts, package registries, model APIs, MCP servers and cloud platforms. This document specifies how an agent authenticates to those services with properties comparable to passkeys, without giving the agent any secret it could leak. It defines one new component, the Agent Authenticator, along with its data formats, ceremonies and bindings to existing OAuth, MCP, git and cloud mechanisms. 1.1. Goals and Non-Goals The mechanism is designed to meet the following goals: 1. The agent process does not hold private keys or any other secret that can be used to obtain tokens. It requests signatures from a separate authenticator. 2. A credential can be used only with the relying party for which it was created. The origin is taken from the network connection rather than from the agent's output, so an agent that has been manipulated through prompt injection cannot direct a credential to another site. 3. Agent keys are generated and held in secure hardware or in an attested cloud key service, and relying parties can learn how well a key is protected through a normalized assurance level. 4. A named person approves each agent credential, and each high-risk action, using a passkey. The person's device need not be the device on which the agent runs. Ganesan Expires 19 May 2027 [Page 3] Internet-Draft Agent Authenticator November 2026 5. Deployment does not require a new identity system. Enterprise identity providers remain the policy authority, and services accept agent credentials through existing OAuth grants. 6. Each action that the authenticator authorizes is recorded in a signed, tamper-evident log that can be exported to existing security monitoring systems. 7. The same protocol is used whether the agent runs on a personal computer or in a cloud environment; only the implementation of the authenticator differs. The following are out of scope: replacing OAuth, OpenID Connect or WebAuthn; agent-to-agent messaging; and assessing whether an agent's output is correct. 1.2. Motivation Coding agents today authenticate with the same bearer secrets humans use (PATs, API keys, npm tokens, cloud keys), stored where the model, its subprocesses and any malware can read them. Evidence from Credential Data * A study by Astrix Security [ASTRIX] of 5,205 open-source MCP servers found 88% need credentials, 53% use static API keys or PATs, only 8.5% use OAuth, and 79% pass keys through environment variables. * GitGuardian [GG-SPRAWL] found 28.65 million newly leaked secrets on public GitHub in 2025, an 81% increase in leaked secrets for AI services, and 24,008 secrets in MCP configuration files, 2,117 of them valid. 1.2.3.
